extracted.intended_audience: fans of Noel Miller, stand-up comedians and internet creators interested in craft and career advice
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and career-level guidance for writing, structuring, performing, and producing stand-up (especially a first hour-long special), plus cross-medium creative strategy drawn from an interview with a working comedian.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to stand-up craft fundamentals
rubrics_metrics.description: "Stand-up is stand-up. You still have to stick to the craft and you can’t trick your way around it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on internet fame or gimmicks to replace strong joke-writing and stagecraft; treat live comedy as a craft that requires disciplined writing, testing, and refinement. Anti-pattern: expecting audience inexperience or platform clout to carry weak material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be authentic / keep to your voice
rubrics_metrics.description: "I kept that as authentic to me as possible..." — authenticity is central to effective stand-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write and perform material that reflects your genuine perspective rather than mimicking idols or pandering for approval. Warning: trying to be liked can lead to inauthentic work that doesn't reflect who you are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with something you are passionate about
rubrics_metrics.description: "The key to having a successful set is starting with something you are passionate about."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin bits and sets from topics you care deeply about — passion helps sell material and sustain long-form work. Use passion as a compass for choosing set openings and anchors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bombing as iterative feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: "Bombing is seen as a negative but really with stand-up... you can try to say something again. Whatever point you’re trying to make, you do have the benefit of time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat failed performances as experiments to refine jokes over multiple shows rather than final verdicts. Iterate material across performances, using audience reactions to adjust timing, tags and delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience familiarity and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When many in the crowd might be first-time stand-up viewers, "it did inform some of the material... acknowledging that kind of just opens up a door and it enables people to be comfortable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor structure and references so new viewers can follow and feel comfortable; this can mean clearer setups, fewer niche in-jokes, and signposting transitions. Anti-pattern: assuming all audience members share the same live-comedy background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain creative control over production when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: "I ultimately want to decide how it’s shot, where it’s shot, and I just wanted the experience of being able to produce my own."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directing/producing your special gives control over visual style and preserves your vision; if possible, work with a trusted crew to realize how material appears on camera. Scoring note: production choices affect audience perception of the set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit cross-medium skills and feed ideas across projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Working in different mediums (short videos, music, podcasts, promos) "feeds into each other" and can provide creative features to add to stand-up and specials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experience from music videos, short films, and promotional material to inspire staging, pacing, and visual motifs in a special. Keep multiple creative avenues open to borrow techniques and fresh material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep experimental channels and avoid pure algorithm-chasing
rubrics_metrics.description: "You’ve voiced your concerns on the 'do what works' world of algorithm chasing... keep an avenue where you’re trying something new and kind of exploring."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance topical, algorithm-friendly content with riskier, craft-focused experiments. Maintain spaces (e.g., live shows or side projects) where you can test new ideas without commercial pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize audience enjoyment over universal likability
rubrics_metrics.description: "I don’t strive to necessarily be liked... a good aim to go for is, 'do people seem to be enjoying it?'. If what you’re making is liked by everyone, I think you gotta question that too."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success by engagement and whether the audience connects, not by trying to please everyone. Allow for polarizing material if it serves your voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build community credibility and respect the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: "Getting passed at clubs is important. But also, just showing the community that you care about it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work to earn respect from fellow comics and venue bookers by taking the craft seriously, showing up, and contributing to the community. Practical steps: consistent club work, supporting peers, and demonstrating professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in long-term craft development rather than short-term cash grabs
rubrics_metrics.description: "I don’t treat this like a cash grab or something. It’s something that is a craft to me and I intend to get sharper at it over time."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on improving material and performance skills over time, even if short-term monetization temptations exist. Anti-pattern: prioritizing quick money over honing material that will stand the test of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage fans respectfully and remain accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: "If people are willing to wait for it, I’m not going to charge them to take a picture... I’ll just do that as like, a bare minimum kind of thing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show gratitude and accessibility to fans (meet-and-greets, selfies, personal interactions) as part of building a loyal audience. Consider trade-offs (time, boundaries) but prioritize genuine appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt tone and approach to each project
rubrics_metrics.description: "With TMG my focus is just more 'What’s like the funniest thing I could say right now?'... personal music is more dramatic/vague."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select tone, structure, and objectives appropriate for the format and collaborators: comedic sketches and network projects prioritize immediate laughs, personal projects may demand nuance and drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance and valuing a slow come-up
rubrics_metrics.description: A slower career progression "gives me a lot of points of reference... you don’t have to be perfect today."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use long-term perspective and prior struggles as stabilizing reference points; perseverance builds resilience and a deeper appreciation for milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use long-form live performance to be vulnerable and tell a story
rubrics_metrics.description: Stand-up "gets to be 100% what I want it to be... it’s easy to open up because I get to sort of craft the points and things I want to get across."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the hour format to develop narrative arcs and deeper vulnerability that shorter internet formats may not allow. Practical: craft beats that build emotional through-lines and allow callbacks.
